title: To be realized
hook: the third truth's task is to be tasted for oneself (SN 56.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: nibbana, the blowing out of greed, hatred and delusion. Your line: the fire goes out.

Try explaining salt to someone who has never tasted it. It's white. It comes in crystals. It makes food taste more like itself. None of that is salt. Then you put a pinch on their tongue, and in half a second they know more than every sentence you said. Some things can be described, and some can only be tasted. The first sermon puts the third truth, the ending of craving, firmly in the second group, and elsewhere the Buddha uses salt to say so.
screen: `EXPLAINING SALT.` → `WHITE, CRYSTALS, SHARP.` → `A PINCH ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Two tasks so far: dukkha is to be understood, craving is to be let go. The third: the ending of craving is sacchikātabba, to be realized. Pali dictionaries build the word from sacchi, before your own eyes, and a verb for making. Made real for yourself, witnessed in person. Not believed on someone's say-so, not admired from a distance. The suttas have a word for the teaching that fits: ehipassiko, come and see. The Buddha doesn't ask anyone to accept the third truth because he said it. He says it can be seen. Now the salt. In the Numbered Discourses, Paharada, a lord of the titans, tells the Buddha what the titans love about the ocean. One of its wonders, he says, is that the great ocean has one taste, the taste of salt. The Buddha answers that just so, this teaching and discipline has one taste, the taste of freedom. Wherever you dip in, the generosity, the precepts, the meditation, the stories, the taste is meant to be the same. So freedom isn't only at the far end of the path, in some final moment. It's a taste, and tastes come in small amounts: a moment when resentment falls away, a morning when you're not chasing anything. Some teachers say those small tastes matter, because they show the third truth isn't just a theory. They're also clear that a pinch isn't the whole ocean.
screen: `SACCHIKĀTABBA: SEEN WITH YOUR OWN EYES.` · `EHIPASSIKO: COME AND SEE.` · `THE OCEAN HAS ONE TASTE.` · `TASTES COME IN SMALL AMOUNTS.` · then, large: `TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: Don't try to manufacture calm; look for a place where peace is already present: the stillness of your hands, the quiet between two sounds, the pause at the bottom of an out-breath. When you find one, stay with it, the way you'd let a flavor sit on your tongue. If it slips away, look for the next one.
Sacchikātabba. To be realized, made real for yourself with your own eyes, the way the ocean's one taste is salt.
Your line: taste it. Some things are only known by tasting. Day three hundred forty-one, done.

howItsDone: Buddhists often recite the qualities of the Dhamma, including that it is to be seen here and now and invites one to come and see; teachers stress testing the teaching in one's own experience.

original.note: Pali sacchikātabba: to be realized, made real with one's own eyes; the third truth's task.

trapdoor: what you thought: realizing something means understanding an idea.
what it means: the third truth is to be witnessed and tasted for yourself, not just thought about.

what a scholar hears: sacchikātabba is formed from sacchi, before one's eyes, and the root kar, to make; AN 8.19 and Udana 5.5 give the simile of the ocean's one taste, vimuttirasa, the taste of freedom.
recall: ending: craving can fade and stop

chat.says: Can you just read about nirvana and understand it?
options: Its task is to be realized: tasted for yourself, like salt, not just read.
Yes, reading the right books about it is the whole of the path.
No, it's hidden, and only the Buddha was ever allowed to know it.
chat.meaning: The first sermon gives the third truth the task sacchikātabba, to be realized, seen with your own eyes. The teaching has one taste: freedom.

sacchikātabba.meaning: to be realized, made real with your own eyes

ehipassiko.meaning: come and see: a word for the teaching

Paharada.meaning: a lord of the titans who praised the ocean's wonders

Numbered Discourses.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's talks arranged by number

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the task of the third truth
AN 8.19 (Paharada Sutta) and Udana 5.5 (Uposatha), the ocean's one taste

notes: Etymology of sacchikātabba (sacchi 'with one's own eyes' + kar 'make') follows standard dictionaries (PED) and is now attributed to them in the script; confirm.

AN 8.19: confirm Pahārāda is the asura lord and the ocean's one taste / vimuttirasa simile; in Udana 5.5 the setting is the uposatha and the monks rather than Pahārāda. The script names Paharada; confirm attribution is fair.
Ehipassiko is from the standard Dhamma recollection formula; confirm.
